bibl.title: Prime time advertisements: Repetition priming from faces seen on subject recruitment posters

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: 1. Repetition priming can be demonstrated for faces shown on advertising posters (Experiments 1-4), although it was reduced in magnitude, as compared with that found for faces encountered in the lab (Experiments 2-4).

span.label: repetition priming of face recognition
span.quote: Repetition priming is defined as a gain in item recognition after previous exposure.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: As in all other experiments in this series, the task at test was a speeded familiarity decision task made to a series of famous and unfamiliar faces.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Repeated exposure strengthens the connections between face recognition units and person identity nodes, so later familiarity decisions are reached faster
span.quote: According to Burton et al.'s (1990) interactive activation (structural) account, repetition priming of faces arises as a result of the strengthening of connections between/ace recognition units (nodes responding to particular individual faces) and person identity nodes (multimodal nodes re sponding to faces, voices, etc.), the proposed locus offa miliarity decisions.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The same link-strengthening process that produces priming is the process by which new faces are learned and stored representations of familiar faces are updated by new exemplars
span.quote: On this account, then, repetition priming taps the same pro cess that underlies the perceptual learning of faces and is the same mechanism by which new faces are learned and representations of familiar faces are modified through encounters with new exemplars.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Priming reflects the ongoing operation of a system that develops and updates the representations used to identify faces, rather than retrieval of the priming episode
span.quote: For the moment, however,we maintain our current hypothesis that priming does reflect the operation of a system mediating the development and updating of the representations used to identify faces.

span.label: Exposure duration and frequency for poster faces were uncontrolled, so absolute priming magnitudes for poster versus lab faces are not directly comparable.
span.quote: This means that we must be cautious about comparing the absolute size ofthe priming obtained from the lab and poster faces.

span.label: Experiment 3 could not counterbalance items across conditions, leaving only four items per cell and an underpowered items analysis.
span.quote: As there were only four items in each cell and counterbalancing was not possible, the items analysis for this experiment lacks power and is not reported.

span.label: The poster-versus-lab comparison in Experiment 1 was severely underpowered.
span.quote: However, the power of this comparison within this exper iment was very low (0.22, assuming a medium effect size, as defined by Cohen, 1977).

span.label: The contextual manipulation used cues known to matter for unfamiliar-face memory, but may not have changed the functional context relevant to identifying familiar faces.
span.quote: However, some caution should also be exercised over these findings, since, although the contextual manipulation in these experiments encompassed changes found to in fluence memory for unfamiliar faces, it is not clear to what extent similar variations capture the functional aspects of the context that are important for the identification of or memory for familiar faces.

span.label: the test list mixed primed faces with unprimed famous faces, unfamiliar faces and six additional familiar filler items
span.note: eliminates: that the priming effect is recognition of fame or familiarity rather than the priming exposure
span.quote: The test list comprised a random sequence of the poster faces, the lab faces, and the unprimed faces, plus six additional familiar filler items.

span.label: repetition priming
span.quote: Repetition priming is the gain in item recognition after earlier exposure to the item

span.label: explicit memory
span.quote: there is little evidence that repeated or extended exposure to items influences repetition priming at all (see Roediger & McDermott's 1993 review), whereas it is clear that increase in exposure duration and/or frequency does affect explicit memory for the items

span.label: episodic memory
span.quote: Half of these subjects were tested on the repetition priming experiment, and half were tested on the test of interference in episodic memory

span.label: context
span.quote: As currently formulated, however, there is no obvious way for structural accounts to explain contextual influences on repetition priming

span.label: **THE PRIME WAS NOT ADMINISTERED - IT WAS A POSTER IN A CORRIDOR.** Faces on subject recruitment advertisements primed laboratory face recognition, `even when the advertisements make no specific mention of experiments involving face recognition` and even when subjects `were not obliged to look at them`. **This is the only record in the corpus where the exposure happened outside the experiment**: dijksterhuis1998 doses by duration, Schmidt2009 by the prime-target gap, bargh1996 by a scrambled-sentence task, and every one of them is delivered by an experimenter to someone who has already consented. Here it happened to people who did not yet know they were in a study
span.quote: Repetition priming was found for both poster and lab faces, although the priming effect was smaller from the poster faces

span.label: **AND THE DISSOCIATION IS IN THE DERIVATIVE, NOT THE LEVEL, WHICH IS A SHARPER CLAIM:** `there is LITTLE EVIDENCE that repeated or extended exposure to items influences REPETITION PRIMING AT ALL ..., WHEREAS it is clear that increase in exposure duration and/or frequency DOES AFFECT EXPLICIT MEMORY for the items.` **More exposure buys explicit memory and buys priming nothing.** Two systems that differ in whether they respond to MORE, rather than in whether they respond - which cannot be explained by one measure being less sensitive, the objection that sinks a difference in means
span.quote: there is little evidence that repeated or extended exposure to items influences repetition priming at all (see Roediger & McDermott's 1993 review), whereas it is clear that increase in exposure duration and/or frequency does affect explicit memory for the items

span.label: **AND THE THEORETICAL GAP IS NAMED AND LEFT OPEN:** `As currently formulated, however, there is NO OBVIOUS WAY for structural accounts to explain contextual influences on repetition priming.` They say what their own result does to the account they favour, and stop. **Second record running to decline to close its own gap** - hesselmann2016 (Q-818) reports its surviving effect as `difficult to reconcile` with the obvious model. A corpus that only held resolved claims would hold neither, and the unresolved version is what a later paper actually picks up
span.quote: As currently formulated, however, there is no obvious way for structural accounts to explain contextual influences on repetition priming

span.label: **AND THE CAREFUL CONCLUSION IS CAREFUL IN A SPECIFIC DIRECTION:** `What we can say, however, is that repetition priming of familiar faces is NOT TRIVIALLY BOUND to the superficial aspects of context that have been found to influence memory for pictures of faces.` **A negative claim about what the effect is NOT bound to**, rather than a positive claim about what carries it. `What we can say, however` is the authors marking the edge of their evidence inside the sentence that states it
span.quote: What we can say, however, is that repetition priming of familiar faces is not trivially bound to the superficial aspects of context that have been found to influence memory for pictures of faces

span.label: replicates → Bruce (1982)
span.quote: The sim ilar performance on same and different exemplars of fa miliar faces replicates Bruce (1982) and probably reflects a ceiling effect.

span.label: extends → Flude (1993)
span.quote: The results presented here suggest that the longevity of face priming (cf. Flude, 1993)does notarise because ofthe maintenance of (at least superficial aspects of) environ mental context.

span.label: extends → Burton et al.'s (1990) interactive activation account
span.quote: However, the interactive activation account, as currently articulated, would not readily accommodate the effects of changes in environ mental context, and, to the extent that priming is, in gen eral, robust from the posters, this supports the model.

span.label: repetition priming —distinct-from→ explicit memory
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — **THE DISSOCIATION IS IN HOW THEY RESPOND TO DOSE, AND THAT IS WHY IT IS STRONG.** Not `priming is smaller than explicit memory` - a difference in means, always answerable with a sensitivity argument - but `more exposure moves one and not the other`. The quote carries both halves and the `whereas`. Weight 0.9 rather than 0.95: the claim is attributed to Roediger & McDermott's 1993 review inside the sentence, so it is the literature's finding that this paper builds on, not this paper's measurement.
span.quote: there is little evidence that repeated or extended exposure to items influences repetition priming at all (see Roediger & McDermott's 1993 review), whereas it is clear that increase in exposure duration and/or frequency does affect explicit memory for the items

span.label: repetition priming —contrasted-with→ episodic memory
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — **A DESIGN SENTENCE, AND IT IS DELIBERATELY THE GROUNDING FOR THIS EDGE.** The two memories are contrasted here by being measured on split halves of the same subject pool from the same poster exposure - which is what makes the later finding (episodic memory weak, priming present) a dissociation rather than a comparison across studies. Weight 0.8: the quote establishes the contrast operationally and not its outcome; the outcome is in the senses and in the record's findings.
span.quote: Half of these subjects were tested on the repetition priming experiment, and half were tested on the test of interference in episodic memory

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: An analysis of variance (ANOVA) on the recognition latencies to familiar faces showed that there was a main effect ofprime [F(2,22) = 13.39,p < .001, by subjects; F(2,21) = 15.55,p < .001, by items]

span.label: t-test
span.quote: (for the comparison between poster and unprimed faces, t = 2.84 by subjects, t= 2.4 by items; bothps < .01).

span.label: p-value
span.quote: showed significantly greater priming for same than for different exemplars [F(l,46) = l7.45,p < .001] and a trend for greater priming in the lab condition than in the poster condition [F(l,46) = 3.11, p = .085] but no other significant effects or interactions (all other ps > .15).

span.label: mean
span.quote: The mean times to make familiarity decisions to the three sets of items in the test phase were as follows: Group 1 (poster), 622 msec (SD= 88 msec); Group 2 (lab), 611 msec (SD= 85 msec); and Group 3 (unprimed), 737 msec (SD= 167 msec).

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: Faces that had been previously seen incidentally on posters were responded to at test with a mean of773 msec (SD= l44msec), compared with 678 msec (SD= 112msec) for faces seen and named initially in the lab and 822 msec (SD = 190 msec) for unprimed faces.

span.label: statistical power / effect size
span.quote: However, the power of this comparison within this exper iment was very low (0.22, assuming a medium effect size, as defined by Cohen, 1977).

span.label: confidence interval
span.quote: Error bars show the within-subjects confidence interval (Loftus & Masson, 1994). 508

span.label: Faces first encountered on subject-recruitment posters outside the laboratory produced measurable repetition priming of laboratory familiarity decisions, even when the poster never mentioned face recognition.
span.quote: Here we show that gains in face recognition in the laboratory are found from faces initially seen in a rather different context on subject recruitment posters, even when the advertisements make no specific mention of experi ments involving face recognition.

span.label: Poster priming was reliable across all four experiments but smaller in magnitude than priming from faces seen in the laboratory.
span.quote: 1. Repetition priming can be demonstrated for faces shown on advertising posters (Experiments 1-4), although it was reduced in magnitude, as compared with that found for faces encountered in the lab (Experiments 2-4).

span.label: Priming survived fully incidental exposure, where participants were never required to look at or name the poster faces.
span.quote: 2. Repetition priming was found even when the faces were presented quite incidentally and subjects were not obliged to look at them (Experiments 2 and 3).

span.label: Changing the pictured exemplar between prime and test reduced priming by about the same amount in the poster and laboratory conditions, so exemplar change and context change acted additively rather than interactively.
span.quote: 3. Changing the pictorial exemplar between the prime and test phases affected priming similarly in lab and on the poster (Experiments 3 and 4). Thus, the effect ofreduced priming after a change ofview is additive with reductions observed after a change in the environmental context within which the faces were primed.

span.label: Changing the background colour behind the face between prime and test had no detectable effect on the size of the priming effect.
span.quote: 5. A change in the background color on which the faces were presented had no measurable effects on the amount of priming (Experiment 4).

span.label: Explicit episodic memory for the poster faces was very poor: they neither interfered as distractors nor were recognised at anything like the rate of laboratory faces.
span.quote: 6. Episodic memory for the faces shown on the poster was weak (Experiments 3 and 4). These faces did not give rise to a sense of familiarity that interfered with their re jection as distractors in a test of memory for faces seen in the lab, and they were recognized very much less well than faces seen in the lab when instructions requested subjects to consider both lab and poster faces as old.

span.label: The authors conclude that face priming does not require reinstating the environmental context of the priming episode, since medium, venue, experimenter presence and task all differed.
span.quote: At a theoretical level, we have demonstrated convinc ingly that repetition priming of faces does not require the reinstatement of the environmental context specifically associated with the experiment itself. The faces on the posters were seen on different material (on paper), in a dif ferent venue, without the experimenter present, and, in some cases (Experiments 2 and 3), with different task de mands from those that were encountered in the laboratory, yet priming was observed in these circumstances.

span.label: A methodological consequence drawn is that researchers testing famous-face recognition must screen out participants who saw those faces in any earlier, apparently unrelated study.
span.quote: Although we cannot conclude that priming will transcend changes in all kinds of context (as we discuss below), our observation of substantial priming even from the posters presenting faces incidentally suggests that anyone whose research tests recognition of famous faces should be care ful to exclude subjects who may previously have seen any of the faces in any other experiments, however unrelated.

span.label: repetition priming
span.quote: Repetition priming is defined as a gain in item recognition after previous exposure.

span.label: episodic account of priming
span.quote: According to episodic accounts of priming (see, e.g., Jacoby, 1983; Roediger & Blaxton, 1987), priming should be stronger the more there is a repetition of stimulus and response processing be tween the prime and test episodes.

span.label: structural models of repetition priming
span.quote: By contrast, structural models of repetition priming (see, e.g., Biederman & Cooper, 1991; Burton, Bruce, & Johnston, 1990; Warren & Morton, 1982) assert that rep etition priming arises as a result of changes within the rep resentational system that is used for the recognition and identification ofwords, objects, or faces.

span.label: context
span.quote: The term context has been used to covera huge range of factors-including environment, interpretation, and mood-provoking Smith, Glenberg, and Bjork (1978) to describe context as "a kind of conceptual garbage can that denotes a great variety of intrinsic and extrinsic char acteristics of the presentation and test of an item (p. 342)."

span.label: place of priming (laboratory versus recruitment poster) and exemplar type (same versus different picture)
span.term: place of priming (laboratory versus recruitment poster) and exemplar type (same versus different picture)
span.quote: The conditions of place of priming (lab vs. poster) and exemplar (same vs. different) were within-subjects factors, but it was not possible to rotate items around the different conditions of this experiment.

span.label: background colour on which faces appeared at test
span.term: background colour on which faces appeared at test
span.quote: In addition to the factors of place of priming and ex emplar type, in this experiment we also manipulated an additional variable-the background color on which the faces appeared at test (which was either the same as or dif ferent from that present during priming).

span.label: poster wording (inviting naming versus purely incidental presentation)
span.term: poster wording (inviting naming versus purely incidental presentation)
span.quote: We compared the effects of the wording on the posters between subjects, although this variable was also con founded with possible differences in the student populations tested at the two universities and other incidental differences in the exper imental set-up.

span.label: speed and accuracy of familiarity decisions to famous faces
span.term: speed and accuracy of familiarity decisions to famous faces
span.quote: We were interested in the relative speed and accuracy of fa miliarity decisions for the three groups of famous faces (poster, lab, and unprimed) at test.

span.label: response-time exclusion window (300-2,000 msec)
span.quote: In this and all subsequent experiments, responses that were made faster than 300 msec or slower than 2,000 msec were excluded from the analysis and counted among the error rates.

span.label: 622 msec / 611 msec / 737 msec — Experiment 1 mean familiarity-decision times for poster-primed, lab-primed and unprimed famous faces
span.quote: The mean times to make familiarity decisions to the three sets of items in the test phase were as follows: Group 1 (poster), 622 msec (SD= 88 msec); Group 2 (lab), 611 msec (SD= 85 msec); and Group 3 (unprimed), 737 msec (SD= 167 msec).

span.label: 773 msec / 678 msec / 822 msec — Experiment 2 mean response times for incidentally poster-primed, lab-primed and unprimed faces, showing significant but weaker poster priming
span.quote: Faces that had been previously seen incidentally on posters were responded to at test with a mean of773 msec (SD= l44msec), compared with 678 msec (SD= 112msec) for faces seen and named initially in the lab and 822 msec (SD = 190 msec) for unprimed faces.

span.label: F(l,46) = l7.45, p < .001 — Experiment 3 effect of same versus different pictorial exemplar on the amount of priming
span.quote: showed significantly greater priming for same than for different exemplars [F(l,46) = l7.45,p < .001] and a trend for greater priming in the lab condition than in the poster condition [F(l,46) = 3.11, p = .085] but no other significant effects or interactions (all other ps > .15).

span.label: 51% — Proportion of poster faces that participants recognised as previously seen in the direct test of episodic memory, against 95% for lab faces
span.quote: They recognized only 51% of the poster faces as having been seen before.

span.label: 95% / 33% / 15% — Replication hit rates for lab faces and poster faces plus the false-positive rate, confirming very weak explicit memory for poster faces
span.quote: These gave hit rates of95% to the faces seen in the lab, 33% to those seen on the poster, and a false positive rate of 15%.
